text: Yes, lots of them. Planets that circle stars other than our Sun are called exoplanets. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] have confirmed more than 6,000 so far, and thousands more are waiting to be checked. Studies suggest that most stars in our [[@milky-way|Milky Way]] [[galaxy|galaxy]] have at least one planet, which means there are probably hundreds of billions of planets in our galaxy alone.

Some are giant balls of gas, some are rocky like Earth, and many are unlike anything in our [[solar-system|solar system]]. Since the first discoveries in the 1990s, finding them has become one of the busiest parts of astronomy.

sec.t:
For centuries people guessed that other stars had planets, but nobody could prove it. Stars are so far away, and so much brighter than any planet, that spotting one is like trying to see a firefly next to a searchlight from thousands of kilometres away.

The first confirmed exoplanets, found in 1992, were odd. They circle a pulsar, the spinning leftover core of a star that exploded. Then, in 1995, two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, found a planet around an ordinary star like the Sun, called 51 Pegasi. The planet was half as heavy as [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] but circled its star in just four days, far closer than [[@mercury-planet|Mercury]] is to our Sun. They won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.

There are two main ways to find exoplanets without seeing them.

The first is the wobble method. As a planet [[orbit|orbits]], its [[gravity|gravity]] tugs its star back and forth very slightly. That wobble shifts the colour of the starlight a tiny bit, which careful instruments can measure. This is how 51 Pegasi b was found.

The second is the transit method. If a planet passes in front of its star, as seen from Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight. Astronomers plot the star's brightness on a graph, and a regular small dip reveals the planet. The size of the dip shows how big the planet is, and the time between dips shows how long its year lasts.

{{story:graphs-charts}}

NASA's Kepler space telescope used transits to find more than 2,600 planets between 2009 and 2018, by staring at about 150,000 stars at once. Its successor, TESS, is surveying nearly the whole sky.

Exoplanets turned out to be far more varied than expected. There are "hot Jupiters", giant gas planets roasting very close to their stars. There are "super-Earths", bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, a size our own solar system doesn't have even though such planets seem common elsewhere.

In 2017, astronomers announced seven Earth-sized planets around a small, cool star called TRAPPIST-1, about 40 [[@light-years|light-years]] away. Several of them may be at the right distance for liquid water. The nearest known exoplanet, Proxima Centauri b, orbits the closest star to the Sun, about 4.2 [[lightyear|light-years]] away.

When a planet passes in front of its star, a little starlight shines through the planet's [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] on its way to us. Different gases soak up different colours of light, leaving tell-tale gaps. By studying that light, astronomers can work out what the air is made of.

The [[@webb-telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]] has already detected water vapour, carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmospheres of several distant planets. One day, a telescope like this might spot a mix of gases on a rocky planet that is hard to explain without [[@alien-life|life]]. Nobody has found that yet, but for the first time in history we have a way to look.

text: Your heart is a [[@muscles|muscle]] about the size of your fist, pumping blood all around your body.

Small animals usually have faster hearts; big animals have slower ones. A mouse's heart can race at around 500 beats a minute, while an elephant's plods along at about 30. Yours, resting, is somewhere in between, and a child's heart usually beats faster than an adult's.
Put two fingers on your wrist and count for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4. That's your heart rate!

d.try: Make a simple stethoscope. Roll a sheet of stiff paper into a tube about 3 cm wide and tape it. Place one end gently on a friend's chest, slightly left of centre, and press your ear to the other end in a quiet room. Listen for the "lub-dub" of their heart.
myth: Your heart is on the left side of your chest.
It sits almost in the middle, behind your breastbone, with its bottom tip angled to the left. That tip gives the strongest thump, which is why we feel the beat more on the left.

sec.t:
Your heart is really two pumps joined together. The right side sends tired blood, low in oxygen, to your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] to pick up fresh oxygen. The left side takes that bright red blood and pushes it out to the rest of your body.

Each side has two rooms, or chambers: a smaller one on top that collects blood and a stronger one below that pumps it out. Flaps called valves snap shut after each push to stop blood flowing backwards. The "lub-dub" sound of a heartbeat is the noise of those valves closing.

At rest, an adult's heart moves about 5 litres of [[@blood|blood]] every minute, roughly the whole body's supply.

The [[@blue-whale|blue whale]] has the largest heart of any animal. One preserved by a museum in Canada weighed about 180 kg, about as much as two grown men. In 2019, scientists stuck a [[sensor|sensor]] on a wild blue whale and found its heart slowed to just 2 beats a minute on deep dives, saving oxygen. At the surface it sped up again to over 30.

At the other end, a flying [[@hummingbirds|hummingbird's]] heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute, faster than you can tap a finger.

Small animals lose heat quickly and burn energy fast, so their hearts must work harder. Big animals are the opposite.

sec.h: A doctor who was too shy
sec.t:
Before 1816, doctors listened to a patient's heart by pressing an ear to their chest. That year, a French doctor named René Laennec felt this was too awkward with a young woman patient. He rolled up a sheet of paper into a tube, put one end on her chest and listened at the other. The heartbeat came through clearly.

He went on to build a wooden tube and called it a stethoscope. Doctors in every hospital from Delhi to Denver still carry its [[descendant|descendant]] around their necks.

Your heart beats about 1 lakh times a day. Over a long life, that adds up to about 3 billion beats. It's hard to picture a number that big, as you can see in [[@big-numbers|big numbers]]. Through all of them, your heart never stops to rest. Between beats, it relaxes for a fraction of a second, and that tiny pause is all the rest it gets.

text: A whistle makes sound by making air wobble very fast. When you blow into a whistle, a narrow jet of air shoots across a hole and hits a sharp edge. The jet can't decide which side of the edge to go, so it flips back and forth, hundreds or thousands of times a second.

Behind the edge is a hollow chamber. The air inside it starts vibrating in time with the flipping jet, making the [[vibration|vibration]] much louder and steadier. That vibration spreads out through the air as [[@sound-travel|sound]].
The size of the chamber sets the note. A small chamber vibrates fast and makes a high, shrill note. A big one vibrates slowly and makes a low, hooting sound.

Dog whistles are pitched mostly above what human ears can hear, but dogs can hear much higher notes than we can. Many dog whistles also make a faint sound that people can hear, especially children, whose ears pick up higher notes than adults' do.

sec.t:
The same idea works in many instruments. A recorder, a flute and a bansuri are all, at heart, whistles. Air is blown against a sharp edge, and a column of air inside the tube vibrates. When a player covers or uncovers holes, they change the length of that air column, and so the note.

Blowing across the top of a bottle works the same way. Your breath flips across the bottle's rim, and the air inside vibrates. Pour in some water, the air space shrinks, and the note rises. Instruments in the same [[@music-instruments-families|family]] as the flute are sometimes called edge-blown instruments for this reason.

In Kongthong, a Khasi village in the hills of [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], mothers make up a short tune for each new baby. The tune becomes that person's name, used alongside their spoken name. Villagers call to each other across the forest using these melodies, which carry further than shouted words.

Elsewhere, people whistle whole sentences. On La Gomera, one of Spain's Canary Islands, shepherds developed Silbo Gomero, a [[@whistled-languages|whistled form of Spanish]], to talk across deep valleys. UNESCO added it to its list of the world's living cultural heritage in 2009, and children on the island learn it at school.

Human [[@ears-hear|ears]] hear notes up to about 20,000 vibrations a second, and fewer as we get older. Dogs can hear notes far higher than that. In 1876, the English scientist Francis Galton made a tiny adjustable whistle to test how high different animals could hear. Dog trainers still use such "silent" whistles, which sound loud to a dog and faint or silent to people.

At home, the whistle you know best may be the one on a pressure cooker. That isn't quite the same thing. Steam pressure lifts a heavy weight on the lid, and the steam rushes out with a shriek. A [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]] counting its whistles is a sound of dinner time in millions of Indian kitchens.

text: पश्मीना मुलायम है, क्योंकि इसके रेशे बेहद पतले होते हैं। ये [[@ladakh|लद्दाख]] के ऊँचे, ठंडे चांगथांग पठार पर रहने वाली चांगथांगी बकरी के भीतरी रोएँ से आते हैं। शून्य से 30 डिग्री नीचे तक गिरने वाली सर्दियाँ झेलने के लिए यह बकरी अपने खुरदुरे बाहरी बालों के नीचे एक महीन, रोएँदार परत उगाती है।

हर रेशा लगभग 12 से 16 माइक्रॉन मोटा होता है। इंसान का बाल लगभग 50 से 100 माइक्रॉन का होता है। पतले रेशे आसानी से मुड़ जाते हैं, इसलिए त्वचा पर चुभने की जगह चिकने लगते हैं। वे हवा की ढेर सारी नन्ही जेबें भी फँसाए रखते हैं, जो [[insulator|कुचालक]] का काम करती हैं। इसीलिए हल्की-सी पश्मीना शॉल भी इतनी गर्म हो सकती है।

sec.t:
बसंत में जब मौसम गर्म होने लगता है, तो बकरियाँ सर्दियों का अपना भीतरी रोआँ गिराने लगती हैं। चरवाहे हर बकरी को पकड़कर हाथ से कंघी करते हुए नरम रेशा निकालते हैं। एक बकरी से साल भर में बस कुछ सौ ग्राम कच्चा रेशा मिलता है, और जब मोटे बाल चुनकर अलग किए जाते हैं तो उसका बड़ा हिस्सा घट जाता है।

एक शॉल बनाने के लिए तीन-चार बकरियों का रेशा लग सकता है। असली पश्मीना के महँगे होने की एक वजह यही है।

कच्चा रेशा कश्मीर पहुँचता है, जहाँ सदियों से ज़्यादातर काम हाथ से होता आया है। पहले उसे साफ़ करके छाँटा जाता है। फिर औरतें उसे लकड़ी के चरखे पर कातती हैं, जिसे *यिंदर* कहते हैं। धागा इतना महीन होता है कि मशीनें उसे तोड़ देती थीं, हालाँकि अब कुछ मशीनें इसे सँभाल लेती हैं।

फिर बुनकर हथकरघों पर कपड़ा बुनते हैं। एक सादी शॉल में कई दिन लग सकते हैं। *कानी* शॉल, जिसमें दर्जनों छोटी लकड़ी की फिरकियों से नमूने बुने जाते हैं, एक साल या उससे भी ज़्यादा ले सकती है। कुछ शॉलों पर बुनाई के बाद *सोज़नी* की हाथ की [[embroidery|कढ़ाई]] होती है, जो लगभग पूरी सतह ढक सकती है।

मुग़ल बादशाह कश्मीरी शॉलों को बहुत कीमती मानते थे और शाही तोहफ़ों में देते थे। 1700 के दशक के आखिर और 1800 के दशक में, जब यात्री और सिपाही इन्हें अपने साथ ले गए, तो यूरोप में इनका जुनून छा गया। कहा जाता है कि फ़्रांस की मलिका जोसेफ़ीन के पास सैकड़ों शॉल थीं।

स्कॉटलैंड के पेज़ली शहर के कारखानों ने मशीनों पर कश्मीरी शॉल के नमूनों की नकल शुरू कर दी। इसीलिए आँसू की बूँद जैसा घुमावदार [[motif|मोटिफ़]], जिसे भारत में *बूटा* या *कलगा* (कैरी) कहते हैं, अंग्रेज़ी में "पेज़ली" कहलाता है। यही नमूना बनारसी रेशम पर भी दिखता है, जो [[@kashmir|कश्मीर]] और वाराणसी की दो बड़ी बुनाई परंपराओं को जोड़ता है।

पश्मीना को कभी-कभी *शहतूश* समझ लिया जाता है, जो तिब्बती हिरण, यानी चीरू, से मिलने वाला और भी महीन ऊन है। शहतूश पाने के लिए हिरण को मारना पड़ता था, और उनकी गिनती तेज़ी से घट गई। अब भारत और दुनिया भर में शहतूश का व्यापार प्रतिबंधित है, और चीरू संरक्षित है।

पश्मीना अलग है। बकरियों को कोई नुकसान नहीं पहुँचता, और कंघी करना पशुपालन की आम ज़िंदगी का हिस्सा है।

"पश्मीना" कहकर बिकने वाली बहुत-सी शॉलें असल में रेशम या ऊन की मिलावट वाली होती हैं, या ऐक्रेलिक से भी बनी होती हैं। 2008 में कश्मीर पश्मीना को भौगोलिक संकेत टैग मिला। तब से श्रीनगर की एक जाँच प्रयोगशाला हाथ से बनी असली शॉलों को प्रमाणित करके उन पर एक खास लेबल लगा सकती है।

जलवायु परिवर्तन और नौजवानों का चरवाही छोड़ना चांगपा समुदाय को चिंता में डालता है। गर्म सर्दियों का मतलब हो सकता है सबसे महीन रेशे वाली बकरियाँ कम होना। बहुत कम कपड़े ऐसे हैं जो इतने सीधे-सीधे ठंड पर टिके हों, और यह बदलाव तेज़ी से हो रहा है।

text: Basavanna, also called Basaveshwara, was a poet, thinker and royal minister who lived in the 12th century in what is now northern [[@karnataka|Karnataka]]. He is remembered for teaching that all people are equal, whatever family or caste they are born into, and that honest work is a kind of worship.

He spread these ideas through *vachanas*, short poems in plain [[@kannada-telugu|Kannada]], the language people spoke at home. Thousands of vachanas survive, written by Basavanna and by the many men and women who joined him.
Today he is honoured as the guiding figure of the Lingayat tradition. People of many backgrounds in Karnataka and beyond quote his lines.

st.prompt: Basavanna's vachanas were written in Kannada, not Sanskrit. Why does that matter?

st.reveal: In Basavanna's day, much religious writing was in Sanskrit, which few people outside a small group could read. Writing in everyday Kannada meant farmers, weavers and cobblers could hear the ideas, remember them and add their own.

sec.t:
Basavanna was probably born in the early 12th century, in a town now called Basavana Bagewadi. Stories say he grew uneasy with [[ritual|rituals]] he felt had lost their meaning, and left home as a young man to study at Kudalasangama, where two rivers meet.

He later went to Kalyana, today's Basavakalyan, capital of King Bijjala II. There he rose to become chief minister, in charge of the treasury. A man close to power, he used that position to argue that the kingdom's ordinary people mattered.

A vachana is a short piece of free verse, with no fixed rhyme or metre, meant to be said or sung. Many of Basavanna's end with the name he used for God, Kudala Sangama Deva, "lord of the meeting rivers". Because they were short and sharp, vachanas were easy to memorise, and many people in Karnataka still know a few by heart.

In one famous vachana he says that the rich build temples for Shiva, but he is poor. So his body will be the temple: his legs the pillars, his body the shrine, his head a dome of gold. The idea was that devotion comes from inside, not from wealth.

This belongs to the wider [[bhakti|bhakti]] movement, in which poets across India spoke to God in their own languages. Later poets in the north, like [[@mirabai-kabir|Kabir and Mirabai]], did something similar.

{{story:mirabai-kabir}}

Basavanna and his companions met in a gathering known as the Anubhava Mantapa, the "hall of experience". There, poets, thinkers and workers discussed religion and how to live. Women spoke as well as men.

Some modern writers call it an early [[parliament|parliament]]. Historians are more careful, because most of what we know comes from texts written centuries later. What seems clear is that people from many backgrounds sat and talked together, which was unusual for the time.

His followers rejected [[@caste-history|caste]] divisions and many temple rituals. Each wore a small personal linga, a symbol of Shiva, on a cord, so worship could happen anywhere.

The story told in later accounts is that Basavanna's circle approved a marriage between a family thought of as high caste and one thought of as low caste. This caused fury at court, and violence followed in Kalyana. Basavanna left and is said to have died at Kudalasangama. The exact details and dates are still debated.

Basava Jayanti, his birth anniversary, is celebrated across Karnataka each spring. A statue of him stands on the bank of the Thames in London, unveiled in 2015. In 2024, the Karnataka government declared him the state's "cultural leader".

His followers, who call themselves Lingayats or Veerashaivas, are one of Karnataka's largest communities. They still debate whether those two names describe the same tradition, and what Basavanna would have thought of later customs. That arguing would probably not have surprised a man who taught people to think for themselves.

text: Blind people use phones with the help of a screen reader, software that reads aloud whatever is on the screen. Every modern smartphone has one built in: VoiceOver on iPhones and TalkBack on Android phones.

With a screen reader turned on, touch works differently. Sliding a finger over the screen makes the phone speak the name of each button or line of text. Swiping left or right moves from one item to the next. A double tap opens whatever was just read out. Users can type by touch and sound, dictate with their voice, or connect a braille keyboard or display.

st.prompt: On a phone with a screen reader turned on, what happens when a blind user touches an app icon once?

options.t: The phone reads out the name of the app, but doesn't open it
The app opens immediately

st.reveal: With a screen reader on, one touch tells you what's under your finger. A double tap anywhere on the screen opens it. This lets blind users explore the screen safely without opening things by mistake.

myth: Blind people can't use touchscreen phones because they can't feel the buttons.
Built-in screen readers turn touchscreens into talking devices. Many blind people use smartphones every day to text, read, shop, travel and take photos.

sec.t:
New users usually start with the voice at normal speed. Over months, many speed it up, until it sounds like a blur to everyone else. Experienced users often listen at two or three times the speed of ordinary speech. The brain adapts, just as a sighted reader learns to skim a page.

Some people also use headphones so their messages aren't read out to the whole bus. Many use a trick called the screen curtain, which turns the display black while the phone still works. It saves battery and stops others peeking.

Phone cameras have become powerful helpers. Apps using [[@computer-vision|computer vision]] can read printed text aloud, describe a scene, recognise banknotes or identify colours of clothes. Some apps connect a blind user by video call with a sighted volunteer, who can read a label or check whether a light is on.

Indian banknotes have small raised marks and different sizes to help people tell them apart. In 2020, the Reserve Bank of India also released an app called MANI that identifies notes using the phone camera.

Maps apps give spoken directions, and some describe what's around a corner. Combined with a white cane or a guide dog, they help many blind people travel on their own.

A screen reader can only read what app makers tell it. If a button has no label, the phone may just say "button", with no clue what it does. Pictures without descriptions are silent. Badly designed apps can be impossible for a blind person to use.

That's why [[@accessibility-tech|accessibility]] is now part of good design. Developers are encouraged to label every button, describe important images and test apps with a screen reader. In many countries, including India and the US, laws require government websites to be accessible to disabled people.

The World Health Organization estimated that about 43 million people worldwide were blind in 2020, and many more have weaker sight. Many live in countries like India, where cheap phones have made a big difference.

Blind people also use computers with screen readers. Free ones like NVDA, made by two blind programmers in Australia, are used around the world. For a lot of blind students, the phone in their pocket has become a library, a map and a scanner all in one.

text: People of Indian origin live in almost every country on Earth. Together they are called the Indian diaspora, a word for a people spread far from their homeland. India's Ministry of External Affairs counted about 3.5 crore in 2024. That includes Indian citizens working abroad and people whose families left India generations ago.

The biggest communities are in the Gulf countries, especially the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, and in the USA, the UK and Canada. There are also old, deep-rooted Indian communities in Mauritius, Fiji, [[@south-africa|South Africa]], Malaysia, Trinidad and Tobago, and Guyana.
According to the United Nations, more people born in India live outside their home country than from any other country: about 1.8 crore in 2020.

sec.t:
In 1834, slavery had just been abolished in the British Empire, and sugar planters needed new workers. The British began shipping labourers from India under contracts called indentures. Workers agreed to labour for about five years, often in harsh conditions, in return for passage and small wages.

Over the next eighty years or so, more than a million Indians made these voyages, to Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana, Suriname, South Africa and elsewhere. They called themselves *girmitiyas*, from their mispronunciation of "agreement". The system ended around 1917. Many never returned. In Mauritius, the stone steps where they landed, Aapravasi Ghat, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Their [[descendant|descendants]] kept festivals, foods and songs alive. Diwali is a public holiday in Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad and Tobago, and Guyana.

{{story:gandhi-south-africa}}

In 1893, a young lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi sailed to South Africa for a job. He saw how Indians there were treated and stayed for over twenty years, leading [[@gandhi-south-africa|peaceful protests]] for their rights. He returned to India on 9 January 1915. That date is now marked as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, a day to honour overseas Indians.

His time abroad shaped the rest of his life. The ideas he tested in South Africa, such as refusing to obey unfair laws without using violence, became the tools of India's freedom struggle. In a sense, one of India's most famous leaders was formed by the diaspora.

From the 1970s, oil money brought huge building projects to the Gulf, and millions of Indian workers followed, especially from Kerala. Cities like [[@dubai|Dubai]] were partly built by them. Most go on work visas and return home after some years, and they send much of their pay back to their families. In some Kerala villages, so many people have worked in the Gulf that new houses, schools and shops were paid for largely with Gulf wages.

In the USA, many Indian engineers, doctors and students arrived after American immigration laws changed in 1965. Indian Americans now number about 5 million. Several have led giant tech firms in [[@silicon-valley|Silicon Valley]], and the astronaut [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]] became the first woman born in India to go to space.

People abroad send home more money than any other diaspora. According to the [[@world-bank-imf|World Bank]], Indians abroad have sent more than US$100 billion a year since 2022, paying for homes, school fees and village businesses.

Ties run the other way too. Families in Toronto watch Indian cricket at odd hours. Children in New Jersey learn [[@marathi-gujarati|Gujarati]] on weekends. A cook in Fiji makes curry with a recipe her great-great-grandmother carried across the ocean, from a village in India she never got to see again.

text: A panchayat is an elected council that runs local affairs in rural India. The word comes from *panch*, meaning five, because village disputes were once settled by a group of five respected elders.

Today panchayats are part of India's [[@democracy-what|democracy]], written into [[@constitution|the Constitution]] since 1992. Villagers elect them every five years. They look after things close to home: village roads, drains, water supply, street lights, local schools and some welfare schemes. Their head is usually called the sarpanch or pradhan.

st.reveal: The gram sabha includes every adult on the village voter list. It can discuss the panchayat's plans and spending, so ordinary villagers get a direct say.

myth: Village councils in India are only for older men.

The Constitution reserves at least a third of panchayat seats, and a third of the head posts, for women. Seats are also reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, so the council reflects the whole village.

sec.h: Three steps from village to district
sec.t:
India's panchayat system has three tiers. The gram panchayat looks after a village or a group of small villages. Above it, the panchayat samiti covers a block, which is a cluster of villages. At the top, the zila parishad covers a whole district.

There are roughly 2.5 lakh gram panchayats. Together, the three tiers have more than 30 lakh elected members, which makes this one of the largest systems of local [[democracy|democracy]] anywhere.

Every gram panchayat answers to a gram sabha, which is a meeting of all the adult voters in the village. The gram sabha can question the panchayat about how money was spent and help choose who should benefit from government schemes. In many villages, though, attendance is low and meetings can be dominated by a few powerful families. Making the gram sabha work well is still a challenge.

sec.h: From an old idea to the Constitution
sec.t:
Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] believed India's freedom should start in its villages. He spoke of *gram swaraj*, or village self-rule, where each village would manage most of its own needs.

{{story:gandhi}}

After independence, the Constitution only asked states to encourage panchayats, so their strength varied a lot. On 2 October 1959, Prime Minister [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]] launched a panchayati raj system in Nagaur district, Rajasthan. Still, many states held panchayat elections rarely or not at all.

That changed with the 73rd Amendment, which came into force on 24 April 1993. It made elections every five years compulsory, set up state election commissions to run them, and reserved seats for women and for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. India now marks 24 April as National Panchayati Raj Day.

Reserving seats for women brought lakhs of them into local government, many for the first time. Studies have found that women leaders often push for things like drinking water and village roads.

There are problems too. In some places, a husband or relative quietly runs the panchayat while the elected woman is leader only in name. This practice is widely criticised, and several states have run training and awareness campaigns to stop it.

A minister in Delhi cannot know which handpump in a village has broken. A panchayat member who lives down the road probably does. Panchayats also get money to spend. Funds come from the central and state governments, and some panchayats collect small local taxes, such as on houses or markets. With it they might build a new drain, repair a school roof or pay workers under rural job schemes. Villagers can ask to see the accounts at the gram sabha. That is the main idea behind panchayats: decisions are often better when they are made close to the people they affect. Cities have their own version, called municipalities. To see the wider picture, read how [[@states-india|India's states]] share power with the centre, or what everyday [[@villages-india|village life]] looks like.

text: Nearly every game uses maths somewhere. Dice games run on [[@probability|probability]], the maths of chance. Card games need counting and memory. Strategy games like chess and noughts and crosses are puzzles about planning ahead, which mathematicians study as [[@game-theory|game theory]]. Sudoku is pure logic with numbers as symbols.
Some games hide the maths so well that you never notice it. Others, like Nim and 21, can be solved completely: once you know the trick, you can win every time.

st.prompt: You roll two ordinary dice and add them. Which total is most likely?

st.reveal: There are 36 ways two dice can land. Six of them add up to 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4 and the reverse of each). Only one way, 6+6, makes 12. That is why so many board games are built around 7.

sec.t:
In one version of Nim, you put 21 matchsticks on a table. Two players take turns removing 1, 2 or 3 sticks. Whoever takes the last stick loses.

The secret lies in the number 4. If you always leave your opponent a number of sticks that is one more than a multiple of 4 (17, 13, 9, 5, and finally 1), they are trapped. Whatever they take, you take enough to make the pair add up to 4. In 1901, an American mathematician named Charles Bouton published the full winning method for the bigger version of Nim with several piles. It uses the [[binary|binary]] number system, the same 0s and 1s that computers use.

sec.h: Chess and the explosion of choices
sec.t:
[[@chess-india|Chess]], which grew from the Indian game chaturanga, looks simple. Yet after just three moves each, the board can be in millions of different positions. The number of possible complete games is so large that it beats the number of [[atom|atoms]] in the observable universe, by most estimates.

That is why nobody, human or computer, can "solve" chess by checking every game. Players learn patterns instead. Computers search millions of positions a second and use clever shortcuts to ignore bad moves.

[[@snakes-ladders|Snakes and ladders]] grew out of gyan chaupar, an old Indian game played with dice or cowrie shells. Ladders stood for virtues like generosity, and snakes for faults like anger. British families took it home in the 1800s, and Americans later sold a version called Chutes and Ladders.

It is a game of pure luck, since players make no choices. But mathematicians have still studied it. Using [[probability|probability]], they can work out how many turns a game lasts on average on a particular board, and which squares players land on most often.

Sudoku asks you to fill a 9 by 9 grid so that each row, column and box has the digits 1 to 9 once. No adding is needed. It is a logic puzzle. An American, Howard Garns, published it in 1979 as Number Place. A Japanese puzzle company renamed it sudoku in the 1980s, and it swept the world in 2005.

Tic-tac-toe, or noughts and crosses, is a solved game too. If both players never make a mistake, it always ends in a draw. Once a child works this out, the game usually stops being much fun. That moment of seeing through a game is also a kind of maths.

text: Chess is very old, but for most of history you needed a partner sitting across the board. The internet changed that. Now you can open an app and get a game in seconds against someone in Chennai, Chicago or Cairo, at any hour.

Several things then pushed chess online into a boom: lockdowns in 2020, a hit TV show, games short enough to play on a bus, and stars who streamed their games live. Chess.com, the biggest site, passed 100 million members in December 2022 and more than 250 million by 2026. India has become one of the busiest chess countries of all.

sec.h: The year everyone was at home
sec.t:
In 2020, schools and offices closed during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]]. People looked for games they could play from home, and chess was ready. Then, in October, Netflix released The Queen's Gambit, a drama about a fictional chess prodigy in 1960s America. Chess sets sold out in some shops, and millions joined chess sites.

That same year, the first Online Chess Olympiad was held. After a final disrupted by internet problems, the gold medal was shared by India and Russia. In early 2023, a fresh rush of players crowded onto Chess.com so quickly that its servers struggled under the load.

Chess turned into something people watch as well as play. [[grandmaster|Grandmasters]] began [[@streaming|streaming]] their games with live chat, talking through each move and joking with viewers. Big online events invited comedians and gamers to compete, which pulled in fans who had never touched a chessboard. Some of this looks a lot like [[@esports|esports]], with commentators, prize money and fan clubs.

Computers changed the game too. Free chess engines, programs far stronger than any human, now check every game in seconds and show the best moves. That helps beginners learn fast. It also creates a problem: some people secretly use engines to cheat, so sites run detection systems to catch suspicious play.

Online chess gives every player a number called a rating. It goes up when you win and down when you lose, and beating a stronger player earns more points than beating a weaker one. The idea comes from Arpad Elo, a Hungarian-American physics teacher whose system was adopted by the world chess federation in 1970.

Because sites match you with people of a similar rating, most games feel close, win or lose. That keeps players coming back for one more game. The very best grandmasters have classical ratings above 2,700, while a keen beginner might start around a few hundred on some sites.

Chess was born in India, in an early form called chaturanga, so its new popularity here feels like a homecoming. [[@viswanathan-anand|Viswanathan Anand]] became India's first grandmaster in 1988 and later world champion, inspiring a generation.

Many of that generation grew up playing thousands of online games. In December 2024, D. Gukesh of Chennai won the world championship at 18, the youngest undisputed champion in history. At the Chess Olympiad in Budapest that year, India won gold in both the open and women's sections. In 2025, Divya Deshmukh won the Women's World Cup. All of them trained with screens as well as boards.

text: Kalaripayattu is a martial art from [[@kerala|Kerala]], on India's south-west coast. It mixes high kicks, leaps, deep crouching stances, weapons and wrestling. The name joins two Malayalam words: kalari, the training ground, and payattu, practice or fighting.

It is very old, though nobody knows quite how old. Legends say the warrior-sage Parashurama taught it. Historians link its present form to the warrior families of [[medieval|medieval]] Kerala, from around the 12th century or later. Today, children and adults train in it for fitness, discipline and sport, and it has appeared in national games and films.

The flexible urumi sword

st.reveal: Students start with meipayattu, body training that builds balance and stretch. Wooden sticks come next, then metal weapons, and the hardest stage, fighting unarmed, comes last. Mastering every stage can take many years.

sec.h: A gym dug into the ground
sec.t:
A traditional kalari is a pit, often about a metre deep and about 13 metres long, a little longer than a city bus. The mud walls block wind and keep the space cool in Kerala's heat. A small shrine sits in one corner, and students touch the ground and the shrine before training.

Fighters usually train in oil-rubbed skin and a simple loincloth or cotton clothes. The oil keeps muscles warm and supple. Some kalaris also give special oil massages, using knowledge of the body that is close to ayurveda.

sec.h: Sticks, daggers and the bendy sword
sec.t:
After years of body training, students move to weapons. They start with wooden sticks of different lengths, then the curved wooden otta, shaped a bit like an elephant's tusk. Later come daggers, spears, swords and shields.

The most famous weapon is the urumi. It is a long, thin band of springy steel, sometimes 1.5 metres or more, and some have several blades. When it isn't in use, it can be coiled around the waist like a belt. Swinging one is dangerous, so only advanced students learn it. Last of all comes verumkai, fighting with bare hands, including ways to stop an armed attacker.

Under British rule, carrying weapons was restricted, and kalaripayattu faded in many places. A revival started in the 1920s, when teachers in northern Kerala began demonstrating it in public again.

Today there are kalaris across Kerala and beyond. Meenakshi Amma of Vadakara, who began training as a small girl, was still teaching in her seventies when she received the Padma Shri, one of India's top civilian honours, in 2017. In 2021, kalaripayattu was added to the Khelo India Youth Games.

sec.h: From the battlefield to the stage
sec.t:
Kalaripayattu has shaped other arts. [[@kathakali|Kathakali]] dancers have long done kalari-style training to build strong legs and control. Film fight scenes in Malayalam, Tamil and Hindi cinema have borrowed its leaps.

Old ballads from northern Kerala, the Vadakkan Pattukal, sing of kalari heroes, including a woman fighter named Unniyarcha. And the strangest part? India has another ancient sport where athletes twist and balance on top of a wooden pole, and [[@sport-mallakhamb|mallakhamb]] can look even harder than kalari.

text: Sprinters run fast because they push down on the ground very hard and very quickly. Each time a foot lands, it presses with a force of several times the runner's body weight, in less than a tenth of a second. That push launches them forward into the next stride.

Strong, springy muscles, mostly the "fast-twitch" kind, make this possible. So do long legs, a perfect start, a relaxed upper body and years of training. The very best put it all together in under 10 seconds.

sec.t:
On 16 August 2009, in Berlin, Usain Bolt of Jamaica ran 100 metres in 9.58 seconds. In 2026 it was still the world record. Between 60 and 80 metres, he was travelling at about 44 km/h, faster than a car in a city school zone.

Bolt is 1.95 metres tall, unusually tall for a sprinter. His long legs meant he took about 41 steps to finish, while most rivals needed 44 or 45. Tall runners usually struggle at the start, but Bolt's power let him catch up.

The women's world record is even older. Florence Griffith-Joyner of the USA ran 10.49 seconds in 1988.

Your [[@muscles|muscles]] contain different kinds of fibres. Slow-twitch fibres are good for long, steady work, like marathon running. Fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and powerfully but tire fast.

Elite sprinters usually have a high share of fast-twitch fibres, partly from their [[gene|genes]] and partly from training. Sprint training builds these muscles with explosive exercises, like jumps, short sprints and heavy lifts.

A 100 m race can be won or lost at the gun. Sprinters crouch in starting blocks, ready to push off. When the gun fires, the sound reaches their ears and their brain sends signals to the muscles.

That takes time. The rules assume no human can react in less than 0.1 seconds, so anyone who leaves the blocks faster is called for a false start, and is usually out of the race. Good sprinters react in about 0.13 to 0.17 seconds, a gap that comes down to the science of [[@sport-science-reaction-time|reaction time]].

Sprint spikes are light shoes with metal pins under the front of the foot. They grip the rubbery track so no push is wasted.

Wind matters too. A tailwind helps, so records only count if the wind behind the runners is no more than 2 metres per second. Modern tracks are springy, giving back some energy with each step.

India's fastest sprinters are closing the gap. In May 2026, Gurindervir Singh ran 100 metres in 10.09 seconds in Ranchi, a new national record, beating a mark set by Animesh Kujur the day before.

Before them came legends like [[@milkha-singh|Milkha Singh]], the "Flying Sikh", who finished fourth in the 400 m at the 1960 Olympics. And yet even Bolt would lose a race to a cheetah, which can reach around 100 km/h in short bursts and is now [[@cheetah-return|running again in India]].

हर बार खाते, पीते, च्युइंग गम चबाते या बोलते समय भी हवा के छोटे-छोटे घूँट खाने के साथ नीचे सरक जाते हैं। सोडे वाले पेय और गैस जोड़ देते हैं, क्योंकि उनमें [[carbon-dioxide|कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड]] घुली होती है। यह हवा और गैस बोतल के बुलबुलों की तरह [[@stomach-digest|पेट]] के ऊपरी हिस्से में उठ जाती है।

sec.t:
खाने की नली, यानी ईसोफ़ेगस, मांसपेशी के एक छल्ले पर पेट से जुड़ती है, जिसे लोअर ईसोफ़ेजियल स्फ़िंक्टर कहते हैं। ज़्यादातर समय यह कसा रहता है, ताकि पेट का [[acid|एसिड]] और खाना उछलकर ऊपर न आए।

जब पेट का ऊपरी हिस्सा गैस से फूलता है, तो [[nerve|नसें]] संकेत भेजती हैं और यह छल्ला थोड़ी देर के लिए ढीला हो जाता है। गैस खाने से हल्की होती है, इसलिए वह पहले ऊपर सरक जाती है। डकार शरीर का दबाव निकालने वाला वाल्व है, कुछ-कुछ प्रेशर कुकर की सीटी जैसा।

जल्दी-जल्दी खाना, पेय गटकना, स्ट्रॉ से पीना और च्युइंग गम चबाना, इन सबसे ज़्यादा हवा निगली जाती है, और ज़्यादा डकारें आती हैं। [[@soft-drinks|सोडे वाले पेय]] तो सबसे बड़े डकार-कारखाने हैं।

sec.h: नन्हे बच्चों को मदद क्यों चाहिए
sec.t:
नन्हे बच्चे दूध पीते समय, खासकर बोतल से, खूब हवा निगल लेते हैं। वे हमेशा अपने-आप उसे डकार से नहीं निकाल पाते, और फँसी हुई हवा उन्हें बेचैन और चिड़चिड़ा कर सकती है।

इसीलिए दूध पिलाने के बाद मम्मी-पापा बच्चे को कंधे से लगाकर सीधा पकड़ते हैं और उसकी पीठ हल्के-हल्के थपथपाते या सहलाते हैं। सीधा रहने से हवा पेट के ऊपरी हिस्से तक उठ आती है, जहाँ से वह निकल सकती है। कभी-कभी इसके साथ थोड़ा दूध भी बाहर आ जाता है, जो बिल्कुल सामान्य है।

[[@cows-india|गायें]], भैंसें, भेड़ें और बकरियाँ इंसानों से कहीं ज़्यादा डकारती हैं। उनके पेट का पहला खाना, रूमेन, खमीर उठाने वाली एक बड़ी टंकी जैसा है। वहाँ के सूक्ष्मजीव सख़्त घास को तोड़ते हैं, और काम करते हुए मीथेन छोड़ते हैं।

गाय यह मीथेन घंटे में कई बार डकार से बाहर निकालती है। मीथेन एक ताकतवर [[greenhouse-gas|ग्रीनहाउस गैस]] है, और इंसानों से जुड़े इसके सबसे बड़े स्रोतों में पालतू मवेशी भी हैं। इसीलिए वैज्ञानिक नए चारे परख रहे हैं, जिनमें समुद्री शैवाल से बना एक चारा भी है, जो गायों की बनाई मीथेन घटा देता है। यह [[@climate-change|जलवायु परिवर्तन]] से लड़ाई का हिस्सा है।

कुछ लोग पाते हैं कि वे डकार ले ही नहीं पाते। इसकी जगह उनके सीने में गुड़गुड़ाहट होती है और पेट दर्द के साथ फूल जाता है। अमेरिका के डॉक्टरों ने इस हालत का ठीक से वर्णन 2019 में ही किया, और अक्सर इसका इलाज हो सकता है।

अगर बहुत ज़्यादा डकारें आएँ और साथ में दर्द, सीने में जलन या निगलने में दिक्कत हो, तो डॉक्टर को बताना ठीक है। पर ज़्यादातर डकारें बस हवा का वहीं लौट जाना है जहाँ से वह आई थी।

खाने की मेज़ पर डकार लेना बदतमीज़ी है या नहीं, यह इस पर निर्भर है कि तुम कहाँ हो और किसके साथ हो। ज़्यादातर भारतीय और अमेरिकी घरों में ज़ोर की डकार के बाद लोग “माफ़ कीजिए” या “एक्सक्यूज़ मी” कहते हैं। नन्हे बच्चों को हर जगह छूट है, और बच्चा बड़ी-सी डकार ले ले, तो ज़्यादातर बड़े अब भी ताली बजा देते हैं।

text: A mummy is a body that has been dried and preserved so that it does not rot. Ancient Egyptians made mummies because they believed a person's spirit needed a body in the [[@myths-egyptian|afterlife]]. The best-known method took about 70 days.

Embalmers removed [[@brain-works|the brain]] and most of the inner organs, then packed the body in natron, a natural salt, for about 40 days to dry it out. After that, they rubbed it with oils and resins and wrapped it in many layers of linen, with lucky charms called amulets tucked between them.

sec.t:
The first Egyptian mummies were made by accident. Over 5,000 years ago, people buried their dead in shallow pits in the hot, dry desert sand. The sand soaked up moisture so fast that the bodies dried before they could decay.

One such body, buried around 3500 BCE, is in the British Museum. Scientists scanned it and found it was a young man who had been stabbed in the back. When later Egyptians began burying important people in coffins and tombs, away from the sand, the bodies rotted. So they developed ways to dry them on purpose.

After drying, the body was stuffed with linen or sawdust to give it shape. Then came wrapping, which could use hundreds of square metres of linen. Priests said prayers as they worked. Amulets, such as a scarab beetle placed over the heart, were meant to protect the dead person on their journey.

A mask was placed over the face. Tutankhamun's famous mask is made of about 10 kg of gold, roughly the weight of a big bucket of water. The mummy was then placed in one or more coffins, sometimes nested like Russian dolls.

Egyptians mummified animals too, in enormous numbers. Cats, ibis birds, crocodiles, falcons and even baboons were preserved as offerings to the gods. Some animal cemeteries hold millions of mummies. Pets were sometimes mummified to join their owners.

Other peoples made mummies too. The Chinchorro people, who fished along the coast of what is now Chile and [[@peru|Peru]], began preserving their dead about 7,000 years ago, two thousand years before the Egyptians. Their mummies, painted black or red, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021. In very cold or very dry places, such as mountains and deserts, nature has also made mummies on its own.

Scientists no longer unwrap mummies. Instead they use [[@x-rays|X-rays]] and CT scanners to look inside without damage. Scans have revealed broken bones, bad teeth, diseases and even what people ate. They showed that Tutankhamun had a damaged foot and probably walked with a cane, and many canes were found in his tomb.

text: On 4 December 1872, the crew of a ship called the *Dei Gratia* spotted another sailing ship zigzagging across the Atlantic, east of the Azores islands. She was the *Mary Celeste*. Nobody was at the wheel. When they rowed over and climbed aboard, they found the ship sound, the cargo nearly all there and about six months of food in the stores. The ten people who should have been on board were gone.

They were never found. The lifeboat was missing, and so were the captain's [[navigation|navigation]] tools. That one clue tells us most of what we know: the crew almost certainly climbed into the small boat and left. Why they would swap a good ship for a tiny open boat in the middle of the ocean is the real mystery.

st.reveal: The food, water and almost all the cargo were still there. The small lifeboat was gone, along with the captain's navigation instruments, which tells us the crew most likely left in a hurry, on purpose.

sec.t:
The ship had a troubled past. She was built in Nova Scotia, Canada, in 1861 and first named *Amazon*. Her first captain fell ill and died on her early voyages, and she later ran aground and was rebuilt before being renamed *Mary Celeste*.

The captain was Benjamin Briggs, an experienced sailor from Massachusetts. With him were his wife Sarah, their two-year-old daughter Sophia, and seven crewmen. They had left New York on 7 November, heading for Genoa in Italy with 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol, the strong kind used in factories, not for drinking.

The last entry in the ship's log was written on 25 November, near Santa Maria island in the Azores. The ship was found ten days later, still sailing roughly the right way, hundreds of kilometres further on. For more than a week, an empty ship had steered itself across the sea, pushed by wind and [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]].

One idea is that alcohol fumes leaked from the barrels. If Briggs smelled them, or heard a bang, he may have feared an explosion and ordered everyone into the lifeboat, tied on a rope, to wait at a safe distance. In 2006 a chemist at University College London built a model hold and showed that alcohol vapour can burn in a sudden, fairly cool flash that leaves little mark.

Another idea is simpler. With a broken pump and a confusing water reading, Briggs may have thought the ship was sinking fast. Land was close. Leaving would have seemed sensible. If the rope snapped or the wind picked up, a small boat could never have caught a sailing ship again.

sec.h: How a story became a legend
sec.t:
In 1884 a young doctor named Arthur Conan Doyle wrote a short story about the ship, calling it the *Marie Celeste*. He added warm tea, a cat asleep and half-eaten breakfasts. None of it was true, but many readers believed it. Three years later Doyle created [[@sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]], and his made-up version of the mystery is still repeated today.

The ship's own ending was strange too. In 1885 her last captain ran her onto a reef near Haiti on purpose, hoping to cheat an insurance company. He was caught. And the *Mary Celeste* is still dragged into stories about the [[@mystery-bermuda|Bermuda Triangle]], even though she was found on the other side of the Atlantic, thousands of kilometres away.

text: The Pushkar fair is two things at once. It is one of the oldest animal markets in India, where herders from across Rajasthan trade camels, horses and cattle on the sand dunes. It is also a Hindu [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]], held around Kartik Purnima, the full moon that usually falls in November.

For about a week, the quiet lakeside town of Pushkar turns into a giant camp. There are tents, food stalls, Ferris wheels, folk musicians and dancers. Foreign photographers jostle with farmers from nearby villages. Pilgrims take a holy dip in Pushkar Lake, which is ringed by 52 bathing steps called ghats.

options.t: Brahma, the creator
Ganesha
Hanuman

st.reveal: Brahma is one of the three great gods in Hindu belief, yet temples to him are rare. The Brahma temple at Pushkar is the most famous of the few that exist, which is one reason pilgrims come.

It is a real livestock market and a religious festival that is centuries old. Herders still come to buy and sell animals, and pilgrims come to bathe in the lake, even though tourists now arrive in large numbers too.

sec.t:
Herders begin walking in days before the fair, some from hundreds of kilometres away. They camp on the dunes with their [[@camels|camels]] and spend long evenings talking prices around small fires. Buyers check an animal's teeth to judge its age, feel its legs and watch how it walks.

To catch a buyer's eye, herders dress camels up. They hang beaded necklaces and anklets on them, and some shave neat patterns into the camel's fur. Horses and cattle are traded too. In recent years a few prize horses and buffaloes have been sold for prices that make headlines, often more than a new car.

Between the trading, the fair holds contests that sound made up. There is a competition for the longest moustache, with entrants twirling whiskers that reach their ears. There is *matka phod*, where teams try to break a clay pot hung high in the air. Camels race across the sand, and sometimes dance to drums.

Visitors from abroad join a tug of war against local teams. Folk singers from the Thar perform late into the night, their songs older than any stage they stand on.

At night the dunes glow with cooking fires. A camel can kneel, fold its long legs and settle onto the cold sand like a parked car. Herders sleep beside their animals, partly for warmth and partly to guard them. By morning, the air smells of woodsmoke, chai and a few thousand camels, and the bargaining starts again before the sun is fully up.

{{story:people-nomads-india}}

For pilgrims, the market is the side show. Hindu tradition says Brahma, the creator god, dropped a lotus flower here and a lake sprang up where it landed. Pushkar's Brahma temple is one of very few in India dedicated to him. On the night of the full moon, crowds bathe in the lake and float small lamps on the water.

The small town is packed with hundreds of temples. Meat and alcohol are not allowed in Pushkar, so the food stalls sell *malpua*, kachori and sweets by the tray.

The fair has a worry. Fewer camels arrive than in the past. Rajasthan had about 3.3 lakh camels in 2012 and about 2.1 lakh by 2019, according to India's livestock [[census|census]]. Trucks and tractors now do the work camels once did. Grazing land has shrunk, and a 2015 Rajasthan law to protect camels also made it harder to sell them outside the state.

Herders at recent fairs say they now bring only a fraction of the animals their fathers did. The government made the camel Rajasthan's state animal in 2014, hoping to help. Some herding families, such as the Raika, now sell camel milk and cheese to earn more from their herds. Their way of life, moving with animals across the [[@desert-life|desert]], is shared by many of India's travelling communities. And there is a gathering even bigger than Pushkar, where crowds so vast they show up in satellite photos meet at the [[@india-wonder-kumbh|Kumbh Mela]].

text: When you cut or bite an apple, you break open millions of tiny cells. Inside some of those cells are natural chemicals called polyphenols. Elsewhere in the cell sits an [[enzyme|enzyme]], a kind of chemical helper, called polyphenol oxidase. In a whole apple they're kept apart.

The knife mixes them together and lets in oxygen from the air. The enzyme then helps oxygen react with the polyphenols, a process called [[oxidation|oxidation]]. That makes new chemicals, which link up into brown [[pigment|pigments]], related to the [[melanin|melanin]] that colours human skin and hair. Within minutes, the white flesh starts to look tanned.

st.reveal: Lemon juice is acidic and full of vitamin C. The acid slows the browning enzyme, and the vitamin C grabs oxygen before it can react. Together they keep the slice pale for hours.

sec.h: Why fruit bothers to do this
sec.t:
Browning isn't a mistake. It's part of the plant's defence. When an insect chews into an apple or a potato, the brown chemicals that form can be bitter or harmful to germs and pests. They may help seal the wound, a bit like a scab.

Many fruits and vegetables do it. Bananas go brown after peeling, and their skins darken in the fridge. Avocados, potatoes, pears, mushrooms and brinjal all brown when cut. Some apple varieties brown slowly because they have less of the enzyme or fewer polyphenols.

There are a few ways to stop browning, and each blocks a different part of the reaction.

Lemon juice works twice over. Its [[acid|acid]] makes the enzyme sluggish, and its [[vitamin|vitamin]] C reacts with oxygen first, protecting the fruit. Pineapple and orange juice work for the same reason. Cold slows the enzyme down, so slices in the fridge brown more slowly. Covering slices or dropping them in water keeps oxygen away. A pinch of salt in water also slows the enzyme.

Heat destroys the enzyme completely. That's why cooks briefly boil some vegetables before freezing them, and why apple pie filling stays golden instead of turning dark brown.

{{story:rust}}

Every leaf of tea starts out green. To make green tea, workers heat the leaves soon after picking, which kills the enzyme and keeps them green. To make black tea, they do the opposite.

In [[@assam-tea|Assam]] and other tea regions, the fresh leaves are wilted, then rolled or crushed to break their cells, just like cutting an apple. They're spread out in the air, where the enzyme turns them coppery brown. Tea makers often call this step [[fermentation|fermentation]], though it's really oxidation. It gives [[@tea|black tea]] its colour, strength and flavour. Raisins, dates and cocoa beans also get some of their brown colour from similar reactions.

Sometimes cooks want food to turn brown. When bread toasts, onions fry or paneer sizzles on a grill, a different reaction makes the colour. Sugars and proteins react together in the heat, a process called the Maillard reaction. It needs no enzyme at all, just high temperature, and it gives toast, roasted coffee and biscuits much of their flavour.

In the 2000s, a company in Canada developed a new kind of apple that barely browns when cut. Scientists used genetic engineering to quieten the genes that tell the fruit to make polyphenol oxidase. The USA approved the first of these apples in 2015, and they went on sale as packaged slices in 2017.

Some people welcome them, saying they could cut food waste, since bruised and browned fruit often gets thrown away. Others prefer fruit bred in traditional ways. Either way, it shows how a single enzyme, controlled by a few [[@genes-family|genes]], decides how your fruit looks.

And the strangest part? Browning is a slow-motion cousin of another oxygen reaction you see on old bicycles and gates. Iron meeting oxygen and water makes the orange crust called [[@rust|rust]].

text: A lot. The [[@united-nations|United Nations]] estimates that in 2022 about 1 billion tonnes of food were wasted by shops, restaurants and homes around the world. That is roughly one fifth of all the food available to shoppers. On top of that, more food is lost on farms, in storage and on the road before it ever reaches a market.

Most of the waste happens at home. On average, each person in the world wastes about 79 kg of food at home every year, about the weight of a grown-up man. Meanwhile, hundreds of millions of people do not get enough to eat.

sec.t:
Waste happens at every step of the food's journey. On farms, fruit may be left unpicked if prices are too low. On the road, [[@tomatoes|tomatoes]] and bananas bruise and rot, especially in hot countries without cold storage. That is why better [[@farm-to-plate|cold chains]] matter.

In shops, food is thrown away when it passes its date or looks less than perfect. In homes, people cook too much, forget leftovers at the back of the fridge, or throw away food that was still fine to eat.

People once assumed food waste at home was mostly a problem in rich countries. The UN's newer data shows that is not true. Homes in middle-income countries, including India, waste similar amounts per person to homes in the United States and Europe.

What differs is where the rest is lost. In poorer places, more food spoils before it reaches the market. In richer places, more is wasted by shops and shoppers. In the US, confusion over labels like "best before" and "use by" leads many people to throw out perfectly safe food.

Wasting food wastes everything used to grow it: water, land, fuel and [[fertiliser|fertiliser]]. Then, in a landfill, buried food rots without air and gives off methane, a strong [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gas]].

The UN estimates that food loss and waste together cause around 8–10% of all the greenhouse gases humans produce. That makes cutting food waste one of the simplest ways to slow [[@climate-change|climate change]].

A surprising amount of food is thrown away just for its looks. Supermarkets in many countries reject [[@food-why-carrots-orange|carrots that are bent]], apples with small marks and potatoes that are oddly shaped, even though they taste exactly the same. Some of this produce never leaves the farm.

A few shops in Europe and the United States now sell "wonky" fruit and vegetables at lower prices. In Indian markets, the sabziwala often sells slightly bruised tomatoes cheaply in the evening, so cooks can turn them into chutney or curry that night.

Countries have agreed on a goal to halve food waste in shops and homes by 2030. Most of the fixes are small. Buying only what you need, serving smaller portions, storing food properly and eating leftovers all help.

Grandparents in many Indian homes already knew these tricks. Yesterday's rice became lemon rice, stale rotis became a crunchy snack, and vegetable peels went to the cow at the gate.

text: The very first kitchen was simply a fire. Early humans cooked over open flames, in caves or outdoors. For many thousands of years after that, most cooking still happened over fire, often on the floor, in a corner of the main room, with smoke drifting through the house.

Over the last two centuries, kitchens changed faster than ever. Iron [[@induction-stoves|stoves]], chimneys, gas and electricity, running water, fridges, pressure cookers and microwaves all arrived. Each one changed how long cooking took, what people ate and who did the work.

myth: Microwaves cook food from the inside out.
Microwaves heat the outer few centimetres of food first. The middle warms up as heat spreads inwards, which is why big dishes need stirring or a rest before eating.

sec.t:
Open fires and chulhas produce a lot of smoke, which fills small rooms. The World Health Organization says smoke from cooking with wood, dung and coal harms the [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] and heart, especially for women and young children who spend the most time near the fire.

That makes cleaner kitchens a health issue too, part of the wider problem of [[@air-pollution|air pollution]]. In 2016 India launched the Ujjwala Yojana, which has given free LPG gas connections to crores of poor households. Many families still go back to the chulha when refills feel too costly.

In Europe and America, cast-iron stoves spread in the 1800s, replacing open hearths. They used less fuel and kept the fire contained. Gas stoves followed in the late 1800s, and electric stoves in the early 1900s.

Electric [[@refrigerator|refrigerators]] became common in American homes in the 1930s and 1940s. In India, fridges, gas stoves and mixer-grinders spread mostly from the 1970s onwards, first in cities and then in towns.

In 1926 an Austrian architect named Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky designed a small, efficient kitchen for new flats in Frankfurt, Germany. She studied how cooks moved and placed everything within a step or two. It had built-in cupboards, a work surface and storage bins. This Frankfurt Kitchen is often called the first fitted kitchen, and most modular kitchens today follow its idea.

In 1945 Percy Spencer, a radar engineer in the United States, noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted near a radar tube. That led to the [[@microwave|microwave]] oven. Early ones were as tall as a refrigerator, but by the 1970s smaller versions were selling to families.

In India, the [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]] became a kitchen hero from the 1960s. It cooks dal and rice much faster and saves fuel. Its [[@whistles|whistle]] is one of the most familiar sounds in Indian homes.

Kitchens changed who did the work too. For most of history, cooking was done mainly by women, often for many hours a day. Machines saved time, and in many homes, men and children now share the cooking. The kitchen is still the heart of many homes, the place where families gather and talk.
